hook: The greatest war in Indian myth was fought between cousins. Their great-uncle commanded one army. And the man who wrote the whole story was grandfather to both sides. To see how, you need one family tree.

beats.narration: The greatest war in Indian myth was fought between cousins. Their great-uncle commanded one army. And the man who wrote the whole story was grandfather to both sides. To see how, you need one family tree.
beats.claim: The Pandavas and Kauravas are cousins, Bhishma is their great-uncle and commands the Kaurava army, and Vyasa is grandfather to both lines.

beats.narration: One note before we start. The Mahabharata exists in many versions and retellings. This video follows Vyasa's Sanskrit epic, the first book called the Adi Parva, as translated into English by Kisari Mohan Ganguli in the 1880s and 90s.
beats.claim: The Ganguli English translation was published between 1883 and 1896.

beats.narration: It begins with Shantanu, king of Hastinapura, of the Kuru dynasty. Shantanu marries Ganga, the river goddess, on one condition: he must never question anything she does.
beats.claim: Shantanu, Kuru king of Hastinapura, marries Ganga on the condition that he never questions her actions.

beats.narration: Ganga gives birth to seven sons and returns each one to the river. When she carries the eighth to the water, Shantanu finally stops her. Ganga leaves, but the eighth son lives. His name is Devavrata.
beats.claim: Ganga gives her first seven sons to the river; Shantanu stops her at the eighth, Devavrata, and she departs.

beats.narration: Years later, Shantanu falls for Satyavati, a fisherman's daughter. Her father agrees to the marriage only if Satyavati's son becomes king. But the heir is Devavrata.
beats.claim: Satyavati's father demands that her son inherit the throne.

beats.narration: So Devavrata makes two vows. He gives up the throne, and he swears never to marry, so no child of his can ever claim it. The vow is so terrible that from then on he's called Bhishma, the one of the terrible oath. His father grants him a boon: he will die only when he chooses to.
beats.claim: Devavrata renounces the throne and vows lifelong celibacy, earning the name Bhishma; Shantanu grants him the boon of choosing the time of his death.

beats.narration: Now here's a detail that changes everything later. Before her marriage, Satyavati already had a son, born to the sage Parashara. That son became a great sage himself. His name is Vyasa. Remember him.
beats.claim: Before marrying Shantanu, Satyavati bore Vyasa to the sage Parashara.

beats.narration: Shantanu and Satyavati have two sons, Chitrangada and Vichitravirya. Chitrangada dies young in battle. Vichitravirya becomes king, and Bhishma goes to find him wives.
beats.claim: Shantanu and Satyavati's sons are Chitrangada, killed in battle, and Vichitravirya, who becomes king.

beats.narration: Bhishma carries off three princesses of Kashi: Amba, Ambika and Ambalika. Amba is in love with another king, so she is let go. Her story comes back for Bhishma, but that's another episode. Ambika and Ambalika marry Vichitravirya.
beats.claim: Bhishma wins the three princesses of Kashi; Amba is released, and Ambika and Ambalika marry Vichitravirya.

beats.narration: Then Vichitravirya dies, with no children. The Kuru line is about to end. Bhishma is bound by his vow and refuses to father an heir. So Satyavati turns to her other son, Vyasa.
beats.claim: Vichitravirya dies childless; Bhishma refuses because of his vow; Satyavati calls on Vyasa.

beats.narration: Through an ancient custom called niyoga, Vyasa fathers children with the two widowed queens. Ambika shuts her eyes in fear, and her son Dhritarashtra is born blind. Ambalika turns pale, and her son Pandu is born pale. A maid of the palace also bears Vyasa a son, the wise Vidura.
beats.claim: By niyoga, Vyasa fathers Dhritarashtra (born blind as Ambika closed her eyes), Pandu (pale as Ambalika turned pale), and Vidura with a maid.

beats.narration: So the three brothers at the centre of the story aren't Shantanu's grandsons by blood at all. They're Vyasa's sons. Hold on to that.

Because Dhritarashtra is blind, Pandu is crowned king. Dhritarashtra marries Gandhari, and they have a hundred sons and one daughter, Duhshala. The eldest son is Duryodhana. These hundred are the Kauravas.
beats.claim: Dhritarashtra and Gandhari have a hundred sons, eldest Duryodhana, and a daughter Duhshala.

beats.narration: Two details about this branch matter later. When Gandhari learns her husband is blind, she blindfolds her own eyes and keeps them covered for life. And Dhritarashtra has one more son, Yuyutsu, born to a maid. When the war comes, Yuyutsu is the one Kaurava who crosses over to fight for the other side.
beats.claim: Gandhari blindfolds herself on learning Dhritarashtra is blind; Dhritarashtra has a son Yuyutsu by a maid, who later sides with the Pandavas.

beats.narration: Pandu marries two queens, Kunti and Madri. Then, while hunting, he shoots a deer that turns out to be a sage named Kindama, in the form of a deer. The dying sage curses him: if Pandu ever lies with a wife, he will die. So Pandu cannot father children. Kunti has a secret gift. As a girl, the sage Durvasa gave her a mantra to call any god and bear his child.
beats.claim: Pandu marries Kunti and Madri; a sage's curse prevents him fathering children; Kunti holds a mantra from Durvasa to summon gods.

beats.narration: Kunti calls on Dharma and bears Yudhishthira. On Vayu, the wind, and bears Bhima. On Indra, and bears Arjuna. She shares the mantra with Madri, who calls the twin Ashvins and bears the twins Nakula and Sahadeva. These five are the Pandavas.
beats.claim: Kunti bears Yudhishthira (Dharma), Bhima (Vayu) and Arjuna (Indra); Madri bears Nakula and Sahadeva by the Ashvins.

beats.narration: The curse comes true. Years later, in the forest, Pandu forgets himself with Madri and dies. Madri follows him onto the funeral pyre, and Kunti brings all five boys back to Hastinapura, to grow up alongside their hundred cousins.
beats.claim: Pandu dies with Madri under the curse; Madri ascends his pyre; Kunti returns with the five sons to Hastinapura.

beats.narration: But Kunti had used the mantra once before, as an unmarried girl. She called the sun god Surya, and bore a son, Karna. Afraid, she set the baby afloat on a river. He was raised by a charioteer. Karna is Kunti's first-born, the eldest Pandava, and he will fight for the Kauravas.
beats.claim: Before marriage Kunti invoked Surya and bore Karna, whom she set adrift; he was raised by a charioteer and fights on the Kaurava side.

beats.narration: The charioteer is Adhiratha, and his wife Radha raises the boy as her own. That's why Karna is also called Radheya, son of Radha. He grows up believing he is a charioteer's son, and Duryodhana becomes his closest friend.
beats.claim: Karna is raised by the charioteer Adhiratha and his wife Radha, hence the name Radheya, and befriended by Duryodhana.

beats.narration: One more link. Kunti's brother is Vasudeva, the father of Krishna. So Krishna, the Pandavas' guide in the war, is their first cousin.
beats.claim: Kunti is the sister of Vasudeva, Krishna's father, making Krishna the Pandavas' cousin.

beats.narration: And the last name on the tree before the war: Draupadi, daughter of King Drupada of Panchala. Arjuna wins her in a contest of archery, and she becomes the wife of all five Pandava brothers.
beats.claim: Arjuna wins Draupadi, daughter of Drupada of Panchala, at her svayamvara, and she marries all five Pandavas.

beats.narration: Now step back and look at the whole tree. The Pandavas and the Kauravas are first cousins, sons of two brothers. Bhishma, who leads the Kaurava army, is great-uncle to both sides. Karna fights against his own half-brothers without knowing it for most of his life.
beats.claim: Pandavas and Kauravas are cousins; Bhishma is great-uncle to both and commands the Kaurava forces; Karna is the Pandavas' half-brother.

beats.narration: And at the very top of the living family sits Vyasa. Grandfather of the Pandavas. Grandfather of the Kauravas. And, according to tradition, the author of the Mahabharata itself.
beats.claim: Tradition credits Vyasa as the composer of the Mahabharata; he is biological grandfather of both Pandavas and Kauravas.

beats.narration: So when the war at Kurukshetra begins, it isn't two kingdoms at war. It's one family. And the man telling you the story is watching his own grandsons fight.

title: The Mahabharata Family Tree in Shadow Puppets | Who Is Related to Whom
description: The Kurukshetra war was fought between cousins, and the man who wrote the Mahabharata is grandfather to both sides. The family tree from Shantanu to the Pandavas and Kauravas, told in shadow puppets. Version followed: Vyasa's Mahabharata (Adi Parva), K. M. Ganguli translation.
